entries.872e5f88c3850b058314b3a3824662713a5d192b: <div sID="gen2264" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Lev.4" sID="Lev.4"/> <div eID="gen2264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2265" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2266" type="x-p"/> This chapter is concerning the sin-offering, which was properly intended to make atonement for a sin committed through ignorance, I. By the priest himself, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.1-Lev.4.12">ver. 1-12</reference>. Or, II. By the whole congregation, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.13-Lev.4.21">ver. 13-21</reference>. Or, III. By a ruler, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22-Lev.4.26">ver. 22-26</reference>. Or, IV. By a private person, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.27-Lev.4.35">ver. 27</reference>, &c.
entries.1fdea7bb3ee7d1b54644dc66a9adf8a13ac00232: <div eID="gen2266" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2265" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Law of the Sin-Offering. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2267" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, If a soul shall sin through ignorance against any of the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">concerning things</hi> which ought not to be done, and shall do against any of them: <hi type="super">3</hi> If the priest that is anointed do sin according to the sin of the people; then let him bring for his sin, which he hath sinned, a young bullock without blemish unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for a sin offering. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he shall bring the bullock unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and shall lay his hand upon the bullock's head, and kill the bullock before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> And the priest that is anointed shall take of the bullock's blood, and bring it to the tabernacle of the congregation: <hi type="super">6</hi> And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood, and sprinkle of the blood seven times before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , before the vail of the sanctuary. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the priest shall put <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the blood upon the horns of the altar of sweet incense before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the tabernacle of the congregation; and shall pour all the blood of the bullock at the bottom of the altar of the burnt offering, which <hi type="italic">is at</hi> the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he shall take off from it all the fat of the bullock for the sin offering; the fat that covereth the inwards, and all the fat that <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the inwards, <hi type="super">9</hi> And the two kidneys, and the fat that <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon them, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away, <hi type="super">10</hi> As it was taken off from the bullock of the sacrifice of peace offerings: and the priest shall burn them upon the altar of the burnt offering. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the skin of the bullock, and all his flesh, with his head, and with his legs, and his inwards, and his dung, <hi type="super">12</hi> Even the whole bullock shall he carry forth without the camp unto a clean place, where the ashes are poured out, and burn him on the wood with fire: where the ashes are poured out shall he be burnt. <div eID="gen2267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2268" type="x-p"/> The laws contained in the first three chapters seem to have been delivered to Moses at one time. Here begin the statutes of another session, another day. From the throne of glory between the cherubim God delivered these orders. And he enters now upon a subject more strictly new than those before. Burnt-offerings, meat-offerings, and peace-offerings, it should seem, had been offered before the giving of the law upon mount Sinai; those sacrifices the patriarchs had not been altogether unacquainted with (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.20">Gen. viii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.20.24">Exod. xx. 24</reference>), and in them they had respect to sin, to make atonement for it, <reference osisRef="Job.1.5">Job i. 5</reference>. But the law being now added <hi type="italic">because of transgressions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Gal. iii. 19</reference>), and having entered, that eventually <hi type="italic">the offence might abound</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Rom. v. 20</reference>), they were put into a way of making atonement for sin more particularly by sacrifice, which was (more than any of the ceremonial institutions) <hi type="italic">a shadow of good things to come,</hi> but the substance is Christ, and that one offering of himself by which he put away sin and <hi type="italic">perfected for ever those who are sanctified.</hi> <div eID="gen2268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2269" type="x-p"/> I. The general case supposed we have, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">v. 2</reference>. Here observe, 1. Concerning sin in general, that it is described to be against <hi type="italic">any of the commandments of the Lord;</hi> for <hi type="italic">sin is the transgression of the law,</hi> the divine law. The wits or wills of men, their inventions or their injunctions, cannot make that to be sin which the law of God has not made to be so. It is said likewise, <hi type="italic">if a soul sin,</hi> for it is not sin if it be not some way or other the soul's act; hence it is called the <hi type="italic">sin of the soul</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.7">Mic. vi. 7</reference>), and it is the soul that is injured by it, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Prov. viii. 36</reference>. 2. Concerning the sins for which those offerings were appointed. (1.) They are supposed to be overt acts; for, had they been required to bring a sacrifice for every sinful thought or word, the task had been endless. Atonement was made for those in the gross, on the day of expiation, once a year; but these are said to be done against the commandments. (2.) They are supposed to be sins of commission, things which ought not to be done. Omissions are sins, and must come into judgment; but what had been omitted at one time might be done at another, and so to obey was better than sacrifice: but a commission was past recall. (3.) They are supposed to be sins committed through ignorance. If they were done presumptuously, and with an avowed contempt of the law and the Law-maker, the offender was to be cut off, and there remained <hi type="italic">no sacrifice for the sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.27">Heb. x. 26, 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.15.30">Num. xv. 30</reference>. But if the offender were either ignorant of the law, as in divers instances we may suppose many were (so numerous and various were the prohibitions), or were surprised into the sin unawares, the circumstances being such as made it evident that his resolution against the sin was sincere, but that he was overtaken in it, as the expression is (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal. vi. 1</reference>), in this case relief was provided by the remedial law of the sin-offering. And the Jews say, "Those crimes only were to be expiated by sacrifice, if committed ignorantly, for which the criminal was to have been cut off if they had been committed presumptuously." <div eID="gen2269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2270" type="x-p"/> II. The law begins with the case of the anointed priest, that is, the high priest, provided he should sin through ignorance; for <hi type="italic">the law made men priests who had infirmity.</hi> Though his ignorance was of all others least excusable, yet he was allowed to bring his offering. His office did not so far excuse his offence as that it should be forgiven him without a sacrifice; yet it did not so far aggravate it but that it should be forgiven him when he did bring his sacrifice. If he sin <hi type="italic">according to the sin of the people</hi> (so the case is put, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">v. 3</reference>), which supposes him in this matter to stand upon the level with other Israelites, and to have no benefit of his clergy at all. Now the law concerning the sin-offering for the high priest is, 1. That he must bring a bullock without blemish for a sin-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">v. 3</reference>), as valuable an offering as that for the whole congregation (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.14">v. 14</reference>); whereas for any other ruler, or a common person, <hi type="italic">a kid of the goats</hi> should serve, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.23">v. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.28">28</reference>. This intimated the greatness of the guilt connected with the sin of a high priest. The eminency of his station, and his relation both to God and to the people, greatly aggravated his offences; see <reference osisRef="Rom.2.21">Rom. ii. 21</reference>. 2. The hand of the offerer must be laid upon the head of the offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.4">v. 4</reference>), with a solemn penitent confession of the sin he had committed, putting it upon the head of the sin-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.21">ch. xvi. 21</reference>. No remission without confession, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">Ps. xxxii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.13">Prov. xxviii. 13</reference>. It signified also a confidence in this instituted way of expiating guilt, as a figure of something better yet to come, which they could not stedfastly discern. He that laid his hand on the head of the beast thereby owned that he deserved to die himself, and that it was God's great mercy that he would please to accept the offering of this beast to die for him. The Jewish writers themselves say that neither the sin-offering nor the trespass-offering made atonement, except for those that repented and believed in their atonement. 3. The bullock must be killed, and a great deal of solemnity there must be in disposing of the blood; for it was <hi type="italic">the blood that made atonement,</hi> and <hi type="italic">without shedding of blood</hi> there was <hi type="italic">no remission,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.4.5-Lev.4.7">v. 5-7</reference>. Some of the blood of the high-priest's sin-offering was to be <hi type="italic">sprinkled seven times before the veil,</hi> with an eye towards the mercy-seat, though it was veiled: some of it was to be put upon the horns of the golden altar, because at that altar the priest himself ministered; and thus was signified the putting away of that pollution which from his sins did cleave to his services. It likewise serves to illustrate the influence which Christ's satisfaction has upon the prevalency of his intercession. The blood of his sacrifice is put upon the altar of his incense and sprinkled before the Lord. When this was done the remainder of the blood was poured at the foot of the brazen altar. By this rite, the sinner acknowledged that he deserved to have his blood thus poured out like water. It likewise signified the pouring out of the soul before God in true repentance, and typified our Saviour's <hi type="italic">pouring out his soul unto death.</hi> 4. The fat of the inwards was to be burnt upon the altar of burnt-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.8-Lev.4.10">v. 8-10</reference>. By this the intention of the offering and of the atonement made by it was directed to the glory of God, who, having been dishonoured by the sin, was thus honoured by the sacrifice. It signified the sharp sufferings of our Lord Jesus, when he was made sin (that is, a sin-offering) for us, especially the sorrows of his soul and his inward agonies. It likewise teaches us, in conformity to the death of Christ, to crucify the flesh. 5. The head and body of the beast, skin and all, were to be carried <hi type="italic">without the camp,</hi> to a certain place appointed for that purpose, and there burnt to ashes, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.11-Lev.4.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. This was very significant, (1.) Of the duty of repentance, which is the putting away of sin as a detestable thing, which our soul hates. True penitents say to their idols, "Get you hence; what have we to do any more with idols?" The sin-offering is called <hi type="italic">sin.</hi> What they did to that we must do to our sins; the body of sin must be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.6">Rom. vi. 6</reference>. (2.) Of the privilege of remission. When God pardons sin he quite abolishes it, casts it behind his back. <hi type="italic">The iniquity of Judah shall be sought for and not found.</hi> The apostle takes particular notice of this ceremony, and applies it to Christ (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.11-Heb.13.13">Heb. xiii. 11-13</reference>), who suffered without the gate, in the place of a skull, where the ashes of dead men, as those of the altar, were poured out.
entries.0d4ac2c635a895b5fee06f307b8c4102c63639ac: <div eID="gen2270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2271" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And if the whole congregation of Israel sin through ignorance, and the thing be hid from the eyes of the assembly, and they have done <hi type="italic">somewhat against</hi> any of the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">concerning things</hi> which should not be done, and are guilty; 14 When the sin, which they have sinned against it, is known, then the congregation shall offer a young bullock for the sin, and bring him before the tabernacle of the congregation. 15 And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands upon the head of the bullock before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and the bullock shall be killed before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> And the priest that is anointed shall bring of the bullock's blood to the tabernacle of the congregation: <hi type="super">17</hi> And the priest shall dip his finger <hi type="italic">in some</hi> of the blood, and sprinkle <hi type="italic">it</hi> seven times before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> before the vail. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he shall put <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the blood upon the horns of the altar which <hi type="italic">is</hi> before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the tabernacle of the congregation, and shall pour out all the blood at the bottom of the altar of the burnt offering, which <hi type="italic">is at</hi> the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he shall take all his fat from him, and burn <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the altar. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he shall do with the bullock as he did with the bullock for a sin offering, so shall he do with this: and the priest shall make an atonement for them, and it shall be forgiven them. <hi type="super">21</hi> And he shall carry forth the bullock without the camp, and burn him as he burned the first bullock: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a sin offering for the congregation. <div eID="gen2271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2272" type="x-p"/> This is the law for expiating the guilt of a national sin, by a sin offering. If the leaders of the people, through mistake concerning the law, caused them to err, when the mistake was discovered an offering must be brought, that wrath might not come upon the whole congregation. Observe, 1. It is possible that the church may err, and that her guides may mislead her. It is here supposed that the whole congregation may sin, and sin through ignorance. God will always have a church on earth; but he never said it should be infallible, or perfectly pure from corruption on this side heaven. 2. When a sacrifice was to be offered for the whole congregation, the elders were to lay their hands upon the head of it (three of them at least), as representatives of the people and agents for them. The sin we suppose to have been some common custom, taken up and used by the generality of the people, upon presumption of its being lawful, which afterwards, upon search, appeared to be otherwise. In this case the commonness of the usage received perhaps by tradition from their fathers, and the vulgar opinion of its being lawful, would not so far excuse them from sin but that they must bring a sacrifice to make atonement for it. There are many bad customs and forms of speech which are thought to have no harm in them, and yet may bring guilt and wrath upon a land, which therefore it concerns the elders both to reform and to intercede with God for the pardon of, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joel ii. 16</reference>. 3. The blood of this sin-offering, as of the former, was to be <hi type="italic">sprinkled seven times before the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.4.17">v. 17</reference>. It was not to be poured out there, but sprinkled only; for the cleansing virtue of the blood of Christ was then and still is sufficiently signified and represented by sprinkling, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Isa. lii. 15</reference>. It was to be sprinkled seven times. Seven is a number of perfection, because when God had made the world in six days he rested the seventh; so this signified the perfect satisfaction Christ made, and the complete cleansing of the souls of the faithful by it; see <reference osisRef="Heb.10.14">Heb. x. 14</reference>. The blood was likewise to be put upon the horns of the incense-altar, to which there seems to be an allusion in <reference osisRef="Jer.17.1">Jer. xvii. 1</reference>, where the sin of Judah is said to be <hi type="italic">graven upon the horns of their altars.</hi> If they did not forsake their sins, the putting of the blood of their sin-offerings upon the horns of their altars, instead of taking away their guilt, did but bind it on the faster, perpetuated the remembrance of it, and remained a witness against them. It is likewise alluded to in <reference osisRef="Rev.9.13">Rev. ix. 13</reference>, where a voice is heard <hi type="italic">from the four horns of the golden altar;</hi> that is, an answer of peace is given to the prayers of the saints, which are acceptable and prevalent only by virtue of the blood of the sin-offering put upon the horns of that altar; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Rev. viii. 3</reference>. 4. When the offering is completed, it is said, <hi type="italic">atonement is made, and the sin shall be forgiven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.4.20">v. 20</reference>. The promise of remission is founded upon the atonement. It is spoken here of the forgiveness of the sin of the whole congregation, that is, the turning away of those national judgments which the sin deserved. Note, The saving of churches and kingdoms from ruin is owing to the satisfaction and mediation of Christ.
entries.f46026e83fccb80eb3d40a75179feaecacecf5d4: <div eID="gen2272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2273" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> When a ruler hath sinned, and done <hi type="italic">somewhat</hi> through ignorance <hi type="italic">against</hi> any of the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God <hi type="italic">concerning things</hi> which should not be done, and is guilty; 23 Or if his sin, wherein he hath sinned, come to his knowledge; he shall bring his offering, a kid of the goats, a male without blemish: <hi type="super">24</hi> And he shall lay his hand upon the head of the goat, and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a sin offering. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and shall pour out his blood at the bottom of the altar of burnt offering. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he shall burn all his fat upon the altar, as the fat of the sacrifice of peace offerings: and the priest shall make an atonement for him as concerning his sin, and it shall be forgiven him. <div eID="gen2273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2274" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. That God takes notice of and is displeased with the sins of rulers. Those who have power to call others to account are themselves accountable to the ruler of rulers; for, as high as they are, there is a higher than they. This is intimated in that the commandment transgressed is here said to be the <hi type="italic">commandment of the Lord his God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22">v. 22</reference>. He is a prince to others, but let him know the Lord is a God to him. 2. The sin of the ruler which he committed through ignorance is supposed afterwards to come to his knowledge (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.23">v. 23</reference>), which must be either by the check of his own conscience or by the reproof of his friends, both which we should all, even the best and greatest, not only submit to, but be thankful for. What we have done amiss we should be very desirous to come to the knowledge of. <hi type="italic">That which I see not, teach thou me, and show me wherein I have erred,</hi> are prayers we should put up to God every day, that though through ignorance we fall into sin we may not through ignorance lie still in it. 3. The sin-offering for a ruler was to be <hi type="italic">a kid of the goats,</hi> not a bullock, as for the priest and the whole congregation; nor was the blood of his sin-offering to be brought into the tabernacle, as of the other two, but it was all bestowed upon the brazen altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.25">v. 25</reference>); nor was the flesh of it to be burnt, as that of the other two, without the camp, which intimated that the sin of a ruler, though worse than that of a common person, yet was not so heinous, nor of such pernicious consequence, as the sin of the high priest, or of the whole congregation. A kid of the goats was sufficient to be offered for a ruler, but a bullock for a tribe, to intimate that the ruler, though <hi type="italic">major singulis—greater than each,</hi> was <hi type="italic">minor universis—less than the whole.</hi> It is bad when great men give bad examples, but worse when all men follow them. 4. It is promised that the atonement shall be accepted and the sin forgiven (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.26">v. 26</reference>), that is, if he repent and reform; for otherwise God swore concerning Eli, a judge in Israel, that the iniquity of his house should not be purged with sacrifice nor offering for ever, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.14">1 Sam. iii. 14</reference>.
entries.1b50f5702cdce06f7354e259ce75d4f29a77f2c1: <div eID="gen2274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2275" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> And if any one of the common people sin through ignorance, while he doeth <hi type="italic">somewhat against</hi> any of the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">concerning things</hi> which ought not to be done, and be guilty; 28 Or if his sin, which he hath sinned, come to his knowledge: then he shall bring his offering, a kid of the goats, a female without blemish, for his sin which he hath sinned. 29 And he shall lay his hand upon the head of the sin offering, and slay the sin offering in the place of the burnt offering. 30 And the priest shall take of the blood thereof with his finger, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and shall pour out all the blood thereof at the bottom of the altar. 31 And he shall take away all the fat thereof, as the fat is taken away from off the sacrifice of peace offerings; and the priest shall burn <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the altar for a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and the priest shall make an atonement for him, and it shall be forgiven him. 32 And if he bring a lamb for a sin offering, he shall bring it a female without blemish. 33 And he shall lay his hand upon the head of the sin offering, and slay it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering. 34 And the priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and shall pour out all the blood thereof at the bottom of the altar: 35 And he shall take away all the fat thereof, as the fat of the lamb is taken away from the sacrifice of the peace offerings; and the priest shall burn them upon the altar, according to the offerings made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and the priest shall make an atonement for his sin that he hath committed, and it shall be forgiven him. <div eID="gen2275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2276" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the law of the sin-offering for a common person, which differs from that for a ruler only in this, that a private person might bring either a kid or a lamb, a ruler only a kid; and that for a ruler must be a male, for the other a female: in all the circumstances of the management of the offering they agreed. Observe, 1. The case supposed: <hi type="italic">If any one of the common people sin through ignorance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.4.27">v. 27</reference>. The prophet supposes that they were not so likely as the great men to <hi type="italic">know the way of the Lord, and the judgment of their God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.4">Jer. v. 4</reference>), and yet, if they sin through ignorance, they must bring a sin-offering. Note, Even sins of ignorance need to be atoned for by sacrifice. To be able to plead, when we are charged with sin, that we did it ignorantly, and through the surprise of temptation, will not bring us off if we be not interested in that great plea, <hi type="italic">Christ hath died,</hi> and entitled to the benefit of that. We have all need to pray with David (and he was a ruler) to be cleansed from <hi type="italic">secret faults,</hi> the errors which we ourselves do not understand or are not aware of, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.12">Ps. xix. 12</reference>. 2. That the sins of ignorance committed by a single person, a common obscure person, did require a sacrifice; for, as the greatest are not above the censure, so the meanest are not below the cognizance of the divine justice. None of the common people, if offenders, were overlooked in a crowd. 3. That a sin-offering was not only admitted, but accepted, even from one of the common people, and an atonement made by it, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.31">v. 31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.35">35</reference>. Here rich and poor, prince and peasant, meet together; they are both alike welcome to Christ, and to an interest in his sacrifice, upon the same terms. See <reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job xxxiv. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen2276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2277" type="x-p"/> II. From all these laws concerning the sin-offerings we may learn, 1. To hate sin, and to watch against it. That is certainly a very bad thing to make atonement for which so many innocent and useful creatures must be slain and mangled thus. 2. To value Christ, the great and true sin-offering, whose blood cleanses from all sin, which it was not possible that the <hi type="italic">blood of bulls and of goats should take away. Now, if any man sin,</hi> Christ is <hi type="italic">the propitiation</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.1-1John.2.2">1 John ii. 1, 2</reference>), not for Jews only, but for Gentiles. And perhaps there was some allusion to this law concerning sacrifices for sins of ignorance in that prayer of Christ's, just when he was offering up himself a sacrifice, <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.</hi>  <chapter eID="Lev.4"/> <div eID="gen2277" type="x-p"/>

entries.2f0b9e63ff072a7793cb05cd68ddd3a360f7c54e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1007"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen1393" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.4.1">Le 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>. Sin Offering of Ignorance.<div eID="gen1393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1007"/><hi type="bold">2. If a soul shall sin through ignorance against any of the commandments of the Lord--</hi>a soul--an individual. All sins may be considered, in a certain sense, as committed "through ignorance," error, or misapprehension of one's true interests. The sins, however, referred to in this law were unintentional violations of the ceremonial laws,--breaches made through haste, or inadvertency of some negative precepts, which, if done knowingly and wilfully, would have involved a capital punishment.<div eID="gen1394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do against any of them--</hi>To bring out the meaning, it is necessary to supply, "he shall bring a sin offering." <div eID="gen1395" type="x-p"/>
entries.fad83b55a5f6df6b664742265391e709ff7fdd87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1008"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.4.3-Lev.4.35">Le 4:3-35</reference>. Sin Offering for the Priest.</title> <div sID="gen1396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1008"/><hi type="bold">3. If the priest that is anointed do sin--</hi>that is, the high priest, in whom, considering his character as typical mediator, and his exalted office, the people had the deepest interest; and whose transgression of any part of the divine law, therefore, whether done unconsciously or heedlessly, was a very serious offense, both as regarded himself individually, and the influence of his example. He is the person principally meant, though the common order of the priesthood was included.<div eID="gen1396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the sin of the people--</hi>that is, bring guilt on the people. He was to take a young bullock (the age and sex being expressly mentioned), and having killed it according to the form prescribed for the burnt offerings, he was to take it into the holy place and sprinkle the atoning blood seven times before the veil, and tip with the crimson fluid the horns of the golden altar of incense, on his way to the court of the priests,--a solemn ceremonial appointed only for very grave and heinous offenses, and which betokened that his sin, though done in ignorance, had vitiated all his services; nor could any official duty he engaged in be beneficial either to himself or the people, unless it were atoned for by blood. <div eID="gen1397" type="x-p"/>
entries.e47f0695d4535ae1bf282ae4e7e40b5b47a75451: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1009"/><div sID="gen1398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1009"/><hi type="bold">11. the skin of the bullock, and all his flesh--</hi>In ordinary circumstances, these were perquisites of the priests. But in the expiation necessary for a sin of the high priest, after the fat of the sacrifice was offered on the altar, the carcass was carried without the camp [Le 4:12], in order that the total combustion of it in the place of ashes might the more strikingly indicate the enormity of the transgression, and the horror with which he regarded it (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.13.12">He 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen1398" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4368c5e6cb2b44dc039cc248ba03103d31ce47e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1010"/><div sID="gen1399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1010"/><hi type="bold">13-21. if the whole congregation of Israel sin through ignorance--</hi>In consequence of some culpable neglect or misapprehension of the law, the people might contract national guilt, and then national expiation was necessary. The same sacrifice was to be offered as in the former case, but with this difference in the ceremonial, that the elders or heads of the tribes, as representing the people and being the principal aggressors in misleading the congregation, laid their hands on the head of the victim. The priest then took the blood into the holy place, where, after dipping his finger in it seven times, he sprinkled the drops seven times before the veil. This done, he returned to the court of the priests, and ascending the altar, put some portion upon its horns; then he poured it out at the foot of the altar. The fat was the only part of the animal which was offered on the altar; for the carcass, with its appurtenances and offals, was carried without the camp, into the place where the ashes were deposited, and there consumed with fire. <div eID="gen1399" type="x-p"/>
entries.33552d6bb9bad6818bd6301331e24af602be2d01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1011"/><div sID="gen1400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1011"/><hi type="bold">22-26. When a ruler hath sinned, and done somewhat through ignorance against any of the commandments--</hi>Whatever was the form of government, the king, judge, or subordinate, was the party concerned in this law. The trespass of such a civil functionary being less serious in its character and consequences than that either of the high priest or the congregation, a sin offering of inferior value was required--"a kid of the goats"; and neither was the blood carried into the sanctuary, but applied only to the altar of burnt offering; nor was the carcass taken without the camp; it was eaten by the priests-in-waiting. <div eID="gen1400" type="x-p"/>
entries.570d2f7593eff430bb596c123ebcb6bced01745e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1012"/><div sID="gen1401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1012"/><hi type="bold">27-34. if any one of the common people sin through ignorance--</hi>In this case the expiatory offering appointed was a female kid, or a ewe-lamb without blemish; and the ceremonies were exactly the same as those observed in the case of the offending ruler [Le 4:22-26]. In these two latter instances, the blood of the sin offering was applied to the altar of burnt offering--the place where bloody sacrifices were appointed to be immolated. But the transgression of a high priest, or of the whole congregation, entailing a general taint on the ritual of the tabernacle, and vitiating its services, required a further expiation; and therefore, in these cases, the blood of the sin offering was applied to the altar of incense [Le 4:6, 17]. <div eID="gen1401" type="x-p"/>
entries.80370e48760f23ba4067ad3d8dca5ad341c46436: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1013"/><div sID="gen1402" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1013"/><hi type="bold">35. it shall be forgiven him--</hi>None of these sacrifices possessed any intrinsic value sufficient to free the conscience of the sinner from the pollution of guilt, or to obtain his pardon from God; but they gave a formal deliverance from a secular penalty (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">He 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">14</reference>); and they were figurative representations of the full and perfect sin offering which was to be made by Christ. <chapter eID="Lev.4"/>

entries.43311034e67321dd2efc64b3306c619a65e24451: <div eID="gen4334" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4335" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4336" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4336" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4335" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4337" type="x-p"/> The law concerning the sin-offering for transgressions committed through ignorance, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.1">Lev 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">Lev 4:2</reference>. For the priest thus sinning, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.3-Lev.4.12">Lev 4:3-12</reference>. For the sins of ignorance of the whole congregation, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.13-Lev.4.21">Lev 4:13-21</reference>. For the sins of ignorance of a ruler, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22-Lev.4.26">Lev 4:22-26</reference>. For the sins of ignorance of any of the common people, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.27-Lev.4.35">Lev 4:27-35</reference>.
entries.75f4c7318024afa80e146eceee40eed98ecf7517: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen4337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4338" type="x-p"/> If a soul shall sin through ignorance - That is, if any man shall do what God has forbidden, or leave undone what God has commanded, through ignorance of the law relative to these points; as soon as the transgression or omission comes to his knowledge, he shall offer the sacrifice here prescribed, and shall not suppose that his ignorance is an excuse for his sin. He who, when his iniquity comes to his knowledge, refuses to offer such a sacrifice, sins obstinately and wilfully, and to him there remains no other sacrifice for sin - no other mode by which he can be reconciled to God, but he has a certain fearful looking for of judgment - which shall devour such adversaries; and this seems the case to which the apostle alludes, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26">Heb 10:26</reference>, etc., in the words above quoted. There have been a great number of subtle questions started on this subject, both by Jews and Christians, but the above I believe to be the sense and spirit of the law.
entries.e204817a1e28cd80724cb3628e16bda9fdbd56da: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4339" type="x-p"/> If the priest that is anointed - Meaning, most probably, the high priest. According to the sin of the people; for although he had greater advantages than the people could have, in being more conversant with the law of God, and his lips should understand and preserve knowledge, yet it was possible even for him, in that time in which the word of God had not been fully revealed, to transgress through ignorance; and his transgression might have the very worst tendency, because the people might be thereby led into sin. Hence several critics understand this passage in this way, and translate it thus: If the anointed priest shall lead the people to sin; or, literally, if the anointed priest shall sin to the sin of the people; that is, so as to cause the people to transgress, the shepherd going astray, and the sheep following after him.
entries.dc58555e940c20518db559fe0833566f1f341797: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen4339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4340" type="x-p"/> Lay his hand upon the bullock's head - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.1.4">Lev 1:4</reference>.
entries.bfcf33f440d246d80f54b758439902cf6ec91f08: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen4340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4341" type="x-p"/> Seven times - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.30">Exo 29:30</reference>. The blood of this sacrifice was applied in three different ways: <div eID="gen4341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4342" type="x-p"/> 1. The priest put his finger in it, and sprinkled it seven times before the veil, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.6">Lev 4:6</reference>. <div eID="gen4342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4343" type="x-p"/> 2. He put some of it on the horns of the altar of incense. <div eID="gen4343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4344" type="x-p"/> 3. He poured the remaining part at the bottom of the altar of burnt-offerings, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.7">Lev 4:7</reference>.
entries.00f149b1bfb927c3c7cf4bb0bad9945cea1d33b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen4344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4345" type="x-p"/> Without the camp - This was intended figuratively to express the sinfulness of this sin, and the availableness of the atonement. The sacrifice, as having the sin of the priest transferred from himself to it by his confession and imposition of hands, was become unclean and abominable, and was carried, as it were, out of the Lord's sight; from the tabernacle and congregation it must be carried without the camp, and thus its own offensiveness was removed, and the sin of the person in whose behalf it was offered. The apostle (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.11-Heb.13.13">Heb 13:11-13</reference>) applies this in the most pointed manner to Christ: "For the bodies of those beasts whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned without the camp. Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate. Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach."
entries.ea9d1c5b4ffa7ad974891f7cc4fb30a40ccd81da: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen4345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4346" type="x-p"/> If the whole congregation of Israel sin - This probably refers to some oversight in acts of religious worship, or to some transgression of the letter of the law, which arose out of the peculiar circumstances in which they were then found, such as the case mentioned <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">1Sam 14:32</reference>, etc., where the people, through their long and excessive fatigue in their combat with the Philistines, being faint, flew on the spoil, and took sheep, oxen, and calves, and slew them on the ground, and did eat with the blood; and this was partly occasioned by the rash adjuration of Saul, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24">1Sam 14:24</reference> : Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening. <div eID="gen4346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4347" type="x-p"/> The sacrifices and rites in this case were the same as those prescribed in the preceding, only here the elders of the congregation, i. e., three of the Sanhedrin, according to Maimonides, laid their hands on the head of the victim in the name of all the congregation.
entries.d09a2052a962b1a176dd2b8b6d3a8c4f87ceead3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen4347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4348" type="x-p"/> When a ruler hath sinned - Under the term נשיא nasi, it is probable that any person is meant who held any kind of political dignity among the people, though the rabbins generally understand it of the king. <div eID="gen4348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4349" type="x-p"/> A kid of the goats was the sacrifice in this case, the rites nearly the same as in the preceding cases, only the fat was burnt as that of the peace-offering. See <reference osisRef="Lev.4.26">Lev 4:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.3.5">Lev 3:5</reference>.
entries.47b9e4f407cdbb173506a58a8401dcaae68e8084: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen4349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4350" type="x-p"/> The common people - עם הארץ am haarets, the people of the land, that is, any individual who was not a priest, king, or ruler among the people; any of the poor or ordinary sort. Any of these, having transgressed through ignorance, was obliged to bring a lamb or a kid, the ceremonies being nearly the same as in the preceding cases. The original may denote the very lowest of the people, the laboring or agricultural classes. <div eID="gen4350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4351" type="x-p"/> The law relative to the general cases of sins committed through ignorance, and the sacrifices to be offered on such occasions, so amply detailed in this chapter, may be thus recapitulated. For all sins and transgressions of this kind committed by the people, the prince, and the priest, they must offer expiatory offerings. The person so sinning must bring the sacrifice to the door of the tabernacle, and lay his hands upon its head, as in a case already referred to, acknowledging the sacrifice to be his, that he needed it for his transgression; and thus he was considered as confessing his sin, and the sin was considered as transferred to the animal, whose blood was then spilt to make an atonement. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Lev.1.4">Lev 1:4</reference> (note). Such institutions as these could not be considered as terminating in themselves, they necessarily had reference to something of infinitely higher moment; in a word, they typified Him whose soul was made an offering for sin, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa 53:10</reference>. And taken out of this reference they seem both absurd and irrational. It is obviously in reference to these innocent creatures being brought as sin-offerings to God for the guilty that St. Paul alludes <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Cor 5:21</reference>, where he says, He (God) made him to be sin (ἁμαρτιαν, a sin-offering) for us Who Knew No Sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God - holy and pure by the power and grace of God, in or through him. And it is worthy of remark, that the Greek word used by the apostle is the same by which the Septuagint, in more than fourscore places in the Pentateuch, translate the Hebrew word הטאה hattaah, sin, which in all those places our translation renders sin-offering. Even sins of ignorance cannot be unnoticed by a strict and holy law; these also need the great atonement: on which account we should often pray with David, Cleanse thou me from secret faults! <reference osisRef="Psa.19.12">Psa 19:12</reference>. How little attention is paid to this solemn subject! Sins of this kind - sins committed sometimes ignorantly, and more frequently heedlessly, are permitted to accumulate in their number, and consequently in their guilt; and from this very circumstance we may often account for those painful desertions, as they are called, under which many comparatively good people labor. They have committed sins of ignorance or heedlessness, and have not offered the sacrifice which can alone avail in their behalf. How necessary in ten thousand cases is the following excellent prayer! "That it may please thee to give us true repentance; to forgive us all our sins, negligences, and ignorances; and to endue us with the grace of thy Holy Spirit, to amend our lives according to thy Holy Word." - Litany.  <chapter eID="Lev.4"/> <div eID="gen4351" type="x-p"/>

entries.f4b6d22295ec59ab9e1c7de59e02e84c959112c1: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.1">Lev 4:1</reference> <div eID="gen1190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1191" type="x-p"/> The Expiatory Sacrifices. - The sacrifices treated of in ch. 1-3 are introduced by their names, as though already known, for the purpose of giving them a legal sanction. But in ch. 4 and 5 sacrifices are appointed for different offences, which receive their names for the first time from the objects to which they apply, i.e., from the sin, or the trespass, or debt to be expiated by them: viz., חטּאת <hi type="italic">sin</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">sin-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">Lev 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.8">Lev 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.14">Lev 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.19">Lev 4:19</reference>, etc.), and אשׁם <hi type="italic">debt</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">debt-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.15-Lev.5.16">Lev 5:15-16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.19">Lev 5:19</reference>); - a clear proof that the sin and debt-offerings were introduced at the same time as the Mosaic law. The laws which follow are distinguished from the preceding ones by the new introductory formula in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.1-Lev.4.2">Lev 4:1-2</reference>, which is repeated in Lev 5:14. This repetition proves that <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2-Lev.5.13">Lev 4:2-5:13</reference> treats of the sin-offerings, and <reference osisRef="Lev.5.14-Lev.5.19">Lev 5:14-19</reference> of the trespass-offerings; and this is confirmed by the substance of the two series of laws.
entries.10fdd7ff11ede5487cf726bc40188b544b039290: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2-Lev.4.13">Lev 4:2-13</reference> <div eID="gen1191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1192" type="x-p"/> The Sin-Offerings. - The ritual prescribed for these differed, with regard to the animals sacrificed, the sprinkling of the blood, and the course adopted with the flesh, according to the position which the person presenting them happened to occupy in the kingdom of God. The classification of persons was as follows: (1) the anointed priest (Lev 4:2-12); (2) the whole congregation of Israel (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.13">Lev 5:13</reference> -21); (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.3">3</reference>) the prince (vv. 22-26); (4) the common people (v. 27- <reference osisRef="Lev.5.13">Lev 5:13</reference>). In the case of the last, regard was also paid to their circumstances; so that the sin-offerings could be regulated according to the ability of the offerer, especially for the lighter forms of sin (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.1-Lev.5.13">Lev 5:1-13</reference>). <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">Lev 4:2</reference> “<hi type="italic">If a soul sin in wandering from any </hi>(מכּל in a partitive sense) <hi type="italic">of the commandments of Jehovah, which ought not to be done, and do any one of them</hi>” (מאחת with מן partitive, cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.4.13">Lev 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22">Lev 4:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.27">Lev 4:27</reference>, lit., anything of one). This sentence, which stands at the head of the laws for the sin-offerings, shows that the sin-offerings did not relate to sin or sinfulness in general, but to particular manifestations of sin, to certain distinct actions performed by individuals, or by the whole congregation. The distinguishing characteristic of the sin is expressed by the term בּשׁגגה (in error). No sins but those committed בּשׁגגה could be expiated by sin-offerings; whilst those committed with a high hand were to be punished by the extermination of the sinner (Num 15:27-31). שׁגגה, from שׁגג = שׁגה to wander or go wrong, signifies mistake, error, oversight. But sinning “<hi type="italic">in error</hi>” is not merely sinning through ignorance (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.13">Lev 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22">Lev 4:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.27">Lev 4:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.18">Lev 5:18</reference>), hurry, want of consideration, or carelessness (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Lev 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.4">Lev 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.15">Lev 5:15</reference>), but also sinning unintentionally (Num 35:11, Num 35:15, Num 35:22-23); hence all such sins as spring from the weakness of flesh and blood, as distinguished from sins committed with a high (elevated) hand, or in haughty, defiant rebellion against God and His commandments. <reference osisRef="Lev.4.3-Lev.4.12">Lev 4:3-12</reference> <hi type="italic">The sin of the high priest</hi>. - The high priest is here called the “anointed priest” (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">Lev 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.5">Lev 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.16">Lev 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.15">Lev 6:15</reference>) on account of the completeness of the anointing with which he was consecrated to his office (<reference osisRef="Lev.8.12">Lev 8:12</reference>); in other places he is called the great (or high) priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.10">Lev 21:10</reference>; Num 35:25, etc.), and by later writers הראשׁ כּהן, the priest the head, or head priest (2Ki 25:18; <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.11">2Ch 19:11</reference>). If he sinned העם לאשׁמת, “to the sinning of the nation,” i.e., in his official position as representative of the nation before the Lord, and not merely in his own personal relation to God, he was to offer for a sin-offering because of his sin an ox without blemish, the largest of all the sacrificial animals, because he filled the highest post in Israel.
entries.953bd61fd34321b4a1051d8d619d94341199aa93: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.4-Lev.4.7">Lev 4:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen1192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1193" type="x-p"/> The presentation, laying on of hands, and slaughtering, were the same as in the case of the other sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.3-Lev.1.5">Lev 1:3-5</reference>). The first peculiarity occurs in connection with the blood (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.5-Lev.4.7">Lev 4:5-7</reference>). The anointed priest was to take (a part) of the blood and carry it into the tabernacle, and having dipped his finger in it, to sprinkle some of it seven times before Jehovah “<hi type="italic">in the face of the vail of the Holy</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.31">Exo 26:31</reference>), i.e., in the direction towards the curtain; after that, he was to put (נתן) some of the blood upon the horns of the altar of incense, and then to pour out the great mass of the blood, of which only a small portion had been used for sprinkling and smearing upon the horns of the altar, at the bottom of the altar of burnt-offering. A sevenfold sprinkling “in the face of the vail” also took place in connection with the sin-offering for the whole congregation, as well as with the ox and he-goat which the high priest offered as sin-offerings on the day of atonement for himself, the priesthood, and the congregation, when the blood was sprinkled seven times before (לפני) the capporeth (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.14">Lev 16:14</reference>), and seven times upon the horns of the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.18-Lev.16.19">Lev 16:18-19</reference>). So too the blood of the red cow, that was slaughtered as a sin-offering outside the camp, was sprinkled seven times in the direction towards the tabernacle (Num 19:4). The sevenfold sprinkling at the feast of atonement had respect to the purification of the sanctuary from the blemishes caused by the sins of the people, with which they had been defiled in the course of the year (see at ch. 16), and did not take place till after the blood had been sprinkled once “against (? upon) the capporeth in front” for the expiation of the sin of the priesthood and people, and the horns of the altar had been smeared with the blood (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.14">Lev 16:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.18">Lev 16:18</reference>); whereas in the sin-offerings mentioned in this chapter, the sevenfold sprinkling preceded the application of the blood to the horns of the altar. This difference in the order of succession of the two manipulations with the blood leads to the conclusion, that in the case before us the sevenfold sprinkling had a different signification from that which it had on the day atonement, and served as a preliminary and introduction to the expiation. The blood also was not sprinkled upon the altar of the holy place, but only before Jehovah, against the curtain behind which Jehovah was enthroned, that is to say, only into the neighbourhood of the gracious presence of God; and this act was repeated seven times, that in the number seven, as the stamp of the covenant, the covenant relation, which sin had loosened, might be restored. It was not till after this had been done, that the expiatory blood of the sacrifice was put upon the horns of the altar, - not merely sprinkled or swung against the wall of the altar, but smeared upon the horns of the altar; not, however, that the blood might thereby be brought more prominently before the eyes of God, or lifted up into His more immediate presence, as <hi type="italic">Hoffmann</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> suppose, but because the significance of the altar, as the scene of the manifestation of the divine grace and salvation, culminated in the horns, as the symbols of power and might. In the case of the sin-offerings for the high priest and the congregation, the altar upon which this took place was not the altar of burnt-offering in the court, but the altar of incense in the holy place; because both the anointed priest, by virtue of his calling and consecration as the mediator between the nation and the Lord, and the whole congregation, by virtue of its election as a kingdom of priests (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>), were to maintain communion with the covenant God in the holy place, the front division of the dwelling-place of Jehovah, and were thus received into a closer relation of fellowship with Jehovah than the individual members of the nation, for whom the court with its altar was the divinely appointed place of communion with the covenant God. The remainder of the blood, which had not been used in the act of expiation, was poured out at the bottom of the altar of burnt-offering, as the holy place to which all the sacrificial blood was to be brought, that it might be received into the earth.
entries.3582dd91971b7cf5a563f6b8162ed79f076edc0f: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.8-Lev.4.10">Lev 4:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen1193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1194" type="x-p"/> The priest was to lift off “all the fat” from the sacrificial animal, i.e., the same fat portions as in the peace-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.3.3-Lev.3.4">Lev 3:3-4</reference>, כּל־חלב is the subject to יוּרם in <reference osisRef="Lev.3.10">Lev 3:10</reference>), and burn it upon the altar of burnt-offering.
entries.89984d9bea9f6a8036f9008e833177223ea23cfd: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.11-Lev.4.12">Lev 4:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen1194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1195" type="x-p"/> The skin of the bullock, and all the flesh, together with the head and the shank and the entrails (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.9">Lev 1:9</reference>) and the foeces, in fact the whole bullock, was to be carried out by him (the sacrificing priest) to a clean place before the camp, to which the ashes of the sacrifices were carried from the ash-heap (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.16">Lev 1:16</reference>), and there burnt on the wood with fire. (On the construction of <reference osisRef="Lev.4.11">Lev 4:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.4.12">Lev 4:12</reference> see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §145, 2). <div eID="gen1195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1196" type="x-p"/> The different course, adopted with the blood and flesh of the sin-offerings, from that prescribed in the ritual of the other sacrifices, was founded upon the special signification of these offerings. As they were presented to effect the expiation of sins, the offerer transferred the consciousness of sin and the desire for forgiveness to the head of the animal that had been brought in his stead, by the laying on of his hand; and after this the animal was slaughtered, and suffered death for him as the wages of sin. But as sin is not wiped out by the death of the sinner, unless it be forgiven by the grace of God, so devoting to death an animal laden with sin rendered neither a real nor symbolical satisfaction or payment for sin, by which the guilt of it could be wiped away; but the death which it endured in the sinner’s stead represented merely the fruit and effect of sin. To cover the sinner from the holiness of God because of his sin, some of the blood of the sacrifice was sprinkled seven times before Jehovah in the holy place; and the covenant fellowship, which had been endangered, was thereby restored. After this, however, the soul, which was covered in the sacrificial blood, was given up to the grace of God that prevailed in the altar, by means of the sprinkling of the blood upon the horns of the altar of incense, that it might receive the forgiveness of sins and reconciliation with God, and the full enjoyment of the blessings of the covenant be ensured to it once more. But the sin, that had been laid upon the animal of the sin-offering, lay upon it still. The next thing done, therefore, was to burn the fat portions of its inside upon the altar of burnt-offering. Now, if the flesh of the victim represented the body of the offerer as the organ of his soul, the fat portions inside the body, together with the kidneys, which were regarded as the seat of the tenderest and deepest emotions, can only have set forth the better part or inmost kernel of the man, the ἔσω ἄνθρωπος (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.22">Rom 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16">Eph 3:16</reference>). By burning the fat portions upon the altar, the better part of human nature was given up in symbol to the purifying fire of the Holy Spirit of God, that it might be purified from the dross of sin, and ascend in its glorified essence to heaven, for a sweet savour unto the Lord (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.31">Lev 4:31</reference>). The flesh of the sin-offering, however, or “the whole bullock,” was then burned in a clean place outside the camp, though not merely that it might be thereby destroyed in a clean way, like the flesh provided for the sacrificial meals, which had not been consumed at the time fixed by the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.17">Lev 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.8.32">Lev 8:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.6">Lev 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.10">Exo 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.34">Exo 29:34</reference>), or the flesh of the sacrifices, which had been defiled by contact with unclean objects (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.19">Lev 7:19</reference>); for if the disposal of the flesh formed an integral part of the sacrificial ceremony in the case of all the other sacrifices, and if, in the case of the sin-offerings, the blood of which was not brought into the interior of the sanctuary, the priests were to eat the flesh in a holy place, and that not “as a portion assigned to them by God as an honourable payment,” but, according to the express declaration of Moses, “to bear and take away (לשׂאת) the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them” (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.17">Lev 10:17</reference>), the burning of the flesh of the sin-offerings, i.e., of the animal itself, the blood of which was not brought into the holy place, cannot have been without significance, or simply the means adopted to dispose of it in a fitting manner, but must also have formed one factor in the ceremony of expiation. The burning outside the camp was rendered necessary, because the sacrifice had respect to the expiation of the priesthood, and the flesh or body of the bullock, which had been made חטּאת by the laying on of the hand, could not be eaten by the priests as the body of sin, that by the holiness of their official character they might bear and expiate the sin imputed to the sacrifice (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.10.17">Lev 10:17</reference>). In this case it was necessary that it should be given up to the effect of sin, viz., to death or destruction by fire, and that outside the camp; in other words, outside the kingdom of God, from which everything dead was removed. But, inasmuch as it was sacrificial flesh, and therefore most holy by virtue of its destination; in order that it might not be made an abomination, it was not to be burned in an unclean place, where carrion and other abominations were thrown (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.40">Lev 14:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.45">Lev 14:45</reference>), but in the clean place, outside the camp, to which the ashes of the altar of burnt-offering were removed, as being the earthly sediment and remains of the sacrifices that had ascended to God in the purifying flames of the altar-fire.<note placement="foot">The most holy character of the flesh of the sin-offering (Lev 6:18.) furnishes no valid argument against the correctness of this explanation of the burning; for, in the first place, there is an essential difference between real or inherent sin, and sin imputed or merely transferred; and secondly, the flesh of the sin-offering was called most holy, not in a moral, but only in a liturgical or ritual sense, as subservient to the most holy purpose of wiping away sin; on which account it was to be entirely removed from all appropriation to earthly objects. Moreover, the idea that sin was imputed to the sin-offering, that it was made sin by the laying on of the hand, has a firm basis in the sacrifice of the red cow (Num 19), and also occurs among the Greeks (see <hi type="italic">Oehler</hi> in Herzog’s Cycl.).</note>
entries.5a86059147a474bb4f6aca66c22606a9f797aff7: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.13-Lev.4.19">Lev 4:13-19</reference> <div eID="gen1196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1197" type="x-p"/> Sin of the whole congregation. - This is still further defined, as consisting in the fact that the thing was hid (נעלּם)<note placement="foot">In the correct editions נעלּם has <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> both here and in <reference osisRef="Lev.5.2">Lev 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.4">Lev 5:4</reference>, as <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi> informs me, according to an old rule in pointing, which required that every consonant which followed a syllable terminating with a guttural should be pointed with <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi>, if the guttural was to be read with a quiescent <hi type="italic">sheva</hi> and not with <hi type="italic">chateph</hi>. This is the case in ויּאסּר in <reference osisRef="Gen.46.29">Gen 46:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.14.6">Exo 14:6</reference>, תּעלּים in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, and other words in the critical edition of the Psalter which has been carefully revised by Bδr according to the Masora, and published with an introduction by <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi>. In other passages, such as בּכל־לּבּי <reference osisRef="Ps.9.2">Psa 9:2</reference>, על־לּשׁנו <reference osisRef="Ps.15.3">Psa 15:3</reference>, etc., the <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> is introduced to prevent the second letter from being lost in the preceding one through the rapidity of reading. - <hi type="italic">Ewald's</hi> conjectures and remarks about this “<hi type="italic">dagesh</hi>, which is found in certain MSS,” is a proof that he was not acquainted with this rule which the Masora recognises.</note> from the eyes of the congregation, i.e., that it was a sin which was not known to be such, an act which really violated a commandment of God, though it was not looked upon as sin. Every transgression of a divine command, whether it took place consciously or unconsciously, brought guilt, and demanded a sin-offering for its expiation; and this was to be presented as soon as the sin was known. The sin-offering, which the elders had to offer in the name of the congregation, was to consist of a young ox, and was to be treated like that of the high priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.14-Lev.4.23">Lev 4:14-23</reference> compared with <reference osisRef="Lev.4.3-Lev.4.12">Lev 4:3-12</reference>), inasmuch as “the whole congregation” included the priesthood, or at any rate was on an equality with the priesthood by virtue of its calling in relation to the Lord. חטא with על signifies to incur guilt upon (on the foundation of) sin (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.5">Lev 5:5</reference>, etc.); it is usually construed with an accusative (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">Lev 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.28">Lev 4:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.5.6">Lev 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.10">Lev 5:10</reference>, etc.), or with בּ, to sin with a sin (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.23">Lev 4:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.42.22">Gen 42:22</reference>). The subject of ושׁחט (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.15">Lev 4:15</reference>) is one of the elders. “<hi type="italic">The bullock for a sin-offering:</hi>” sc., the one which the anointed priest offered for his sin, or as it is briefly and clearly designated in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.21">Lev 4:21</reference>, “the former bullock” (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.12">Lev 4:12</reference>).
entries.6a097dd760a582b551a662f6ae920640101d0bd8: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.20-Lev.4.21">Lev 4:20-21</reference> <div eID="gen1197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1198" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And let the priest make an atonement for them, that it may be forgiven them,</hi>” or, “so will they be forgiven.” This formula recurs with all the sin-offerings (with the exception of the one for the high priest), viz., <reference osisRef="Lev.4.26">Lev 4:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.31">Lev 4:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.35">Lev 4:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.10">Lev 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.13">Lev 5:13</reference>; Num 15:25-26, Num 15:28; also with the trespass-offerings, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.16">Lev 5:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.18">Lev 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.22">Lev 19:22</reference>, - the only difference being, that in the sin-offerings presented for defilements cleansing is mentioned, instead of forgiveness, as the effect of the atoning sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Lev.12.7-Lev.12.8">Lev 12:7-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.13.20">Lev 13:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.53">Lev 13:53</reference>; Num 8:21). <div eID="gen1198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1199" type="x-p"/> The sin of a ruler. - Lev 4:22. אשׁר: ὅτε, <hi type="italic">when</hi>. נשׂיא is the head of a tribe, or of a division of a tribe (Num 3:24, Num 3:30, Num 3:35).
entries.4c6089596a50dc7e10334ffea4ed5e5a883e70c6: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.23-Lev.4.26">Lev 4:23-26</reference> <div eID="gen1199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1200" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">If</hi> (או, see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §155, 2) <hi type="italic">his sin is made known to him,</hi>” i.e., if any one called his attention to the fact that he had transgressed a commandment of God, he was to bring a he-goat without blemish, and, having laid his hand upon it, to slay it at the place of burnt-offering; after which the priest was to put some of the blood upon the horns of the altar of burnt-offering, and pour out the rest of the blood at the foot of the altar, and then to burn the whole of the fat upon the altar, as in the case of the peaceoffering (see <reference osisRef="Lev.3.3-Lev.3.4">Lev 3:3-4</reference>), and thus to make atonement for the prince on account of his sin. עזים שׂעיר, or שׂעיר alone (lit., hairy, shaggy, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.11">Gen 27:11</reference>), is the buck-goat, which is frequently mentioned as the animal sacrificed as a sin-offering: e.g., that of the tribe-princes (Num 7:16., <reference osisRef="Lev.15.24">Lev 15:24</reference>), and that of the nation at the yearly festivals (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.9">Lev 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.15">Lev 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.19">Lev 23:19</reference>; Num 28:15, Num 28:22, Num 28:30; Num 29:5, Num 29:16.) and at the consecration of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.3">Lev 9:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.9.15">Lev 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.10.16">Lev 10:16</reference>). It is distinguished in Num 7:16. from the <hi type="italic">attudim</hi>, which were offered as peace-offerings, and frequently occur in connection with oxen, rams, and lambs as burnt-offerings and thank-offerings (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.9">Psa 50:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.13">Psa 50:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.66.15">Psa 66:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Isa 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.18">Eze 39:18</reference>). According to <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, עזים שׂעיר, or שׂעיר, was an old he-goat, the hair of which grew longer with age, particularly about the neck and back, and עזים שׂעירת (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.28">Lev 4:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.5.16">Lev 5:16</reference>) an old she-goat; whilst עתּוּד was the younger he-goat, which leaped upon the does (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.10">Gen 31:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.12">Gen 31:12</reference>), and served for slaughtering like lambs, sheep, and goats (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">Deu 32:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.40">Jer 51:40</reference>). But as the עזים שׂעיר was also slaughtered for food (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.31">Gen 37:31</reference>), and the skins of quite young he-goats are called שׂעירת (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.23">Gen 27:23</reference>), the difference between שׂעיר and עתּוּד is hardly to be sought in the age, but more probably, as <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi> supposes, in some variety of species, in which case <hi type="italic">seir</hi> and <hi type="italic">seirak</hi> might denote the rough-haired, shaggy kind of goat, and <hi type="italic">attud</hi> the buck-goat of stately appearance.
entries.2c2a35c65bb0370ba0ad81aadfb8b00181e1f080: <reference osisRef="Lev.4.27-Lev.4.35">Lev 4:27-35</reference> <div eID="gen1200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1201" type="x-p"/> In the case of the <hi type="italic">sin of a common Israelite</hi> (“of the people of the land,” i.e., of the rural population, <reference osisRef="Gen.23.7">Gen 23:7</reference>), that is to say, of an Israelite belonging to the people, as distinguished from the chiefs who ruled over the people (2Ki 11:18-19; 2Ki 16:15), the sin-offering was to consist of a shaggy she-goat without blemish, or a ewe-sheep (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.32">Lev 4:32</reference>). The ceremonial in both cases was the same as with the he-goat (Lev 4:23.). - “<hi type="italic">According to the offerings made by fire unto the Lord</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.35">Lev 4:35</reference>): see at Lev 3:5.  <chapter eID="Lev.4"/> <div eID="gen1201" type="x-p"/>

entries.9d271940dcc0b76c3c585eda919ff16bbce5e1fc: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.4.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.4.1" sID="gen13039" type="section"/> <div sID="gen13040" type="x-p"/>After Moses had treated of the offerings and other sacrifices, which were testimonies of gratitude and exercises of piety, he now descends to the sin-offering (<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">expiationem</hi></foreign>) which held the chief place amongst the sacrifices, inasmuch as, without reconciliation, there could never be any intercourse between men and God; for since He deservedly abominates the whole human race on account of the corruption of our nature, and because we all continually provoke His wrath, the whole hope of salvation must needs be founded on the remedies provided for propitiating Him. This principle, being established, we must remember that Moses will henceforth speak of the expiatory sacrifices which propitiate God to men by the removal of their guilt. He here shews how God is to be appeased, where a man shall have sinned through ignorance or inconsiderateness; wherein too a distinction is laid down between different persons, since one kind of victim is required of a king, another of the priests, and another of ordinary persons; whilst regard is had to the poor, that they may not be burdened by so great an expense as the rich. But, since it will appear from the context that all kinds of ignorance are not here included, we must see what the word <foreign xml:lang="he">שגגה</foreign>, <hi type="italic">shegagah,</hi> <note n="256"> <div sID="gen13041" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">S.M.</hi> says the word means, “a sin into which the perplexed mind has been driven under the impulse of some passion, through thoughtlessness, imprudence, or error, when inattentive to the dictates of reason and of the Spirit.” — <hi type="italic">W</hi>.<div eID="gen13041" type="x-p"/> </note> means, which I have preferred rendering error rather than ignorance; for Moses does not refer to those transgressions into which we are ensnared, when we are led astray by the appearance of rectitude, so as to think ourselves without blame; but to those of which we take no heed, and whereby our minds are not pricked; or to those sudden falls, wherein the infirmity of the flesh so stifles the reason and the judgment as to blind the sinner. It is of such that Paul speaks when he bids us<div eID="gen13040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13042" type="x-p"/>"restore in the spirit of meekness those who <lb/> are overtaken in a fault,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.1">Galatians 6:1</reference>;)<div eID="gen13042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13043" type="x-p"/>for he does not mean those who are deceived by their good intentions (as they call it,) or rather by their foolish opinion, so as to be unconscious of their sin; but those who fall through the infirmity of their flesh, and whom Satan catches unawares in his snares; or who, at any rate, do not perceive the evil they have done, so as immediately to apply the remedy. This will be more clearly understood from <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.19.12 Bible:Ps.19.13">Psalm 19:12, 13</reference>, where David, having asked pardon for his errors, seeks to be kept free from presumptuous sins. <note n="257"> <div sID="gen13044" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">A superbiis</foreign>.” —<hi type="italic"> Lat. “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr">De ses fiertes, et rebellions</foreign>.” — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen13044" type="x-p"/> </note> The antithesis between <foreign xml:lang="he">שגיאות</foreign>, <hi type="italic">shegioth,</hi> <note n="258"> <div sID="gen13045" type="x-p"/> Lexicographers make no distinction between the approximate roots <foreign xml:lang="he">שגג</foreign> and <foreign xml:lang="he">שגה</foreign>. Hence <foreign xml:lang="he">שגיאות</foreign>, is regarded as meaning the same as the word used in <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.2">Leviticus 4:2</reference>. By <foreign xml:lang="he">זדים</foreign>, are understood sins committed with a high hand and rebellious spirit. — <hi type="italic">W.</hi><div eID="gen13045" type="x-p"/> </note> and <foreign xml:lang="he">זדים</foreign>, <hi type="italic">zedim, </hi>shews that those transgressions are called errors, in which there is no criminal pride against God. “If a soul shall sin —<hi type="italic"> from all </hi>the commandments,” <note n="259"> <div sID="gen13046" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">A. V.,</hi> “against any of the commandments.” Ainsworth’s version is, “A soule, when it shall sin through ignorance of all the commandments,” etc.; and his Gloss. “<hi type="italic">of</hi> <hi type="italic">all, </hi>understand, <hi type="italic">by doing any one of all the commandments. </hi>So Moses himself explaineth it in the words here following, and in <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.13 Bible:Lev.4.22 Bible:Lev.4.27">ver. 13, 22, 27</reference>."<div eID="gen13046" type="x-p"/> </note> is a harsh expression; and therefore some refer it to sins of omission, but I interpret it more simply, “If he sin by turning away from the commandments,” or “if he commit any thing opposed (<hi type="italic">alienum</hi>)<hi type="italic">to </hi>the commandments."<div eID="gen13043" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.4.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen13039" osisID="Lev.4.1" type="section"/>
entries.44cc99800583bb8fb6cf48a912794a8fcdfc1fd5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.4.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.4.3" sID="gen13047" type="section"/> <div sID="gen13048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">If the priest that is anointed.</hi> He now distinguishes between different persons, and begins with the high priest, who alone bore the high distinction of the holy unction, unless it be thought better to apply it to the whole supreme class. <note n="260"> <div sID="gen13049" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sur toute la maison d’Aaron</foreign>.” — <hi type="italic">Fr.</hi><div eID="gen13049" type="x-p"/> </note> It is probable, however, that it only refers to one. The more illustrious was his dignity, the more diligently and zealously ought his life to be confirmed to the model of holiness; and therefore the infirmity which was more tolerable in others, was more exceedingly reprehensible in him. This is the reason why it was required that he should atone for himself with a greater victim.
